fatal_errors: The proposed Al0.1CoCrFeNi alloy is not the studied FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayer made from Al0.2CrFeNi and Al targets.
The key transition occurs in the 16 nm-period multilayer with semicoherent interfaces, not in a material defined simply by coherent interfaces.
The generated high-temperature, 500 MPa, 100-hour creep conditions are invented; the study used room-temperature, 5 mN nanoindentation creep.

The mechanism is reversed: coherent interfaces transmit dislocations relatively readily, whereas semicoherent interfaces block and pile up dislocations and are proposed to enable diffusion or interface-slip creep through stress-induced interfacial disorder or amorphization.
The claimed 20–30% creep-resistance improvement and its falsification threshold have no evidentiary basis.
explanation: The hypothesis recognizes that interface coherency can affect dislocation mobility and creep, and its statement that coherent interfaces permit easier dislocation motion has limited qualitative agreement with the target. However, it identifies the wrong alloy, interface state, intervention, loading regime, baseline, and transition direction. The relevant material is the approximately 1 μm-thick FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayer with a 16 nm modulation period (M16), whose semicoherent interfaces contain misfit dislocations. These interfaces strongly obstruct glide, promote pileups and localized stress, and were proposed to facilitate interfacial amorphization, atomic diffusion, or interface slip. M16 consequently showed the lowest stress exponents and strongest reported room-temperature nanoindentation creep resistance relative to coherent M8 and grain-boundary-dominated M32/M80. With no cited evidence and several arbitrary quantitative claims, the generated hypothesis is unsupported rather than a reconstruction.
